items.title: DADR
items.text:
Record human decisions in a simple file format. Implement the data analysis using any tools you like. Assess conformity of the code with decisions automatically.

DADR workflow: draft, review, accept or reject, then audit, report, or supersede Draft • Write a data analysis decisionfrom scratch• Ask an LLM to read an existingcode base and identify key decisions Review Only a human analyst is allowed toapprove or reject decision records Accept Reject Audit • Substantive review: humans must agreewith all decisions• Code review: AI ensures that the codefaithfully implements decisions Report • Methods section• Decision tables• Onboarding documents Supersede • Revert a past decision• Tweak a previous choice

items.title: Problem 1: Opacity
items.text:
Every data analysis rests on dozens of choices: which observations to include, how to code key variables, which model to fit, how to quantify uncertainty. These choices matter: Many Analysts studies show that independent teams given the same data and hypotheses routinely reach different results.1

Most of these choices never appear in a methods section, and reconstructing them from code and data after the fact is an archeology project.

A simple way to record what was decided, why, what alternatives were considered, and what the consequences are.

items.title: Problem 2: Drift
items.text:
On long projects, analysts lose track of key decisions and the reasons behind them. The code drifts from the original intent, and minor-looking choices can change how results are interpreted. The risk grows when analysis is delegated to coding agents, which produce a lot of hard-to-review code.

A human-approved, auditable, and authoritative record of the key decisions made in a project.

items.title: Solution: Data Analysis Decision Records
items.text:
Data Analysis Decision Records (DADR) are designed to make our key analytical choices explicit. Each decision becomes a short Markdown record, stored alongside the code, data, and prose of a project. The DADR markdown files are human-editable, LLM-readable, and version-controllable. They include meta-data fields and tags that enable external tools to track decision flows, audit the faithfulness of a codebase to recorded decisions, and generate reports and narratives directly from the decision ledger.

DADR is not meant to be a comprehensive record of every thought, but rather a focused ledger of the key decisions that shape an analysis. It is a simple specification inspired by the Architecture Decision Record, a proven and popular development practice in the software engineering community.

Every candidate decision must be approved by the human analyst before it enters the permanent record.

Reviewing a candidate in the dadrock web UI.

items.title: New possibilities
items.text: A complete, structured trace of analytic decisions is more than documentation. It is an asset that downstream tools and humans can act on.

items.title: Faithfulness
items.text: Compare code, plan, and manuscript against recorded decisions to flag drift, undocumented choices, or contradictions. An LLM walks the relevant code paths and produces a discrepancy report for human triage.

items.title: Compliance
items.text: Cross-check decisions against a Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), a Pre-Analysis Plan (PAP), Pre-registration, or data cleaning plan to surface deviations and unexecuted commitments.

items.title: Multiverse and robustness
items.text: Automatically surface the choices that need to be subjected to sensitivity, robustness, or multiverse analysis.

items.title: Decision flow
items.text: Follow how analytic choices evolved: which decisions replaced which, when, and why.

items.title: Drafting
items.text: Generate methods sections, appendices, and decision tables directly from the trace, with citations back to the records.

items.title: Onboarding
items.text: Hand a collaborator or new contributor a readable narrative instead of a code-archaeology assignment.

items.title: Replication and reuse
items.text: Give independent analysts a self-contained rationale for every consequential choice.

items.title: Coverage and audit
items.text: Report which analysis activities are backed by decisions, which are unreviewed, and which have gone stale.

items.title: Teaching
items.text: Use real annotated analyses to show how defensible alternatives were considered and chosen.

items.title: Example
items.text:
---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: accepted
id: 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333
tags:
  - kind/sample
  - confidence/high
---

## Context

The randomization log is missing the treatment field for 47 of 8,213
respondents. Without an assignment we cannot estimate either
intent-to-treat or per-protocol effects for those rows. This extends
the sampling rule established in [[01938b8e4d70]].

## Decision

> #axis/sample/complete-case
> Drop the 47 respondents without recorded treatment assignment from
> the analysis sample.

## Alternatives

- Multiple imputation of the assignment indicator (rejected: assignment
  is a treatment, not a covariate; imputing it would invent
  counterfactual exposures).
- Coding the missing rows as control (rejected: silently biases the ITT
  estimate toward the null).

## Consequences

The analysis sample drops from 8,213 to 8,166. Power calculations need
to be re-run; see [[01938c30b1e2]].
Documentation Software

  1. Many Analysts studies:

    • Silberzahn et al. (2018), "Many Analysts, One Data Set: Making Transparent How Variations in Analytic Choices Affect Results," Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1(3): 337–356, doi:10.1177/2515245917747646.
    • Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), "Variability in the Analysis of a Single Neuroimaging Dataset by Many Teams," Nature 582: 84–88, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9.
    • Huntington-Klein et al. (2021), "The Influence of Hidden Researcher Decisions in Applied Microeconomics," Economic Inquiry 59(3): 944–960, doi:10.1111/ecin.12992.
    • Breznau et al. (2022), "Observing Many Researchers Using the Same Data and Hypothesis Reveals a Hidden Universe of Uncertainty," PNAS 119(44): e2203150119, doi:10.1073/pnas.2203150119.

    ↩

items.title: Data Analysis Decision Records
items.text: A Data Analysis Decision Record answers one question: what did we decide, and why? Keep one Markdown file per consequential choice, alongside your analysis.

items.title: Four sections
items.text:
• Context: the question and relevant evidence.
  • Decision: what you chose, stated directly.
  • Alternatives: other approaches considered and why you set them aside.
  • Consequences: implications, tradeoffs, and follow-up work.

A file also has three required YAML fields: title, status, and id. Dadrock generates the ID for you. Tags and links are optional; you do not need a classification system to get started.

items.title: Draft, review, preserve
items.text:
A new record is a candidate. A human reviews it and marks it accepted or rejected. Acceptance keeps the same ID. An agent may help draft a candidate, but cannot decide whether you endorse it.

Once approved, a decision's substantive content is preserved. Changing the decision creates a replacement linked to the original; minor corrections remain possible. The original remains accepted and its successors field names its replacements. “Superseded” describes an accepted record with successors, not a fourth stored status. Dadrock offers a superseded filter for convenience.

items.title: What deserves a record?
items.text:
Start with choices a collaborator would ask you to explain: who enters the sample, how a variable is defined, why a model was chosen, or how missing values are handled. Skip routine formatting and mechanical refactoring. A few useful explanations are better than an unmanageable review queue.

Code can reveal what an analysis does without revealing why. When a draft says the rationale is unknown, supply it or leave the record as a candidate until you can review it.

Install dadrock and record your first decision, or consult the full specification for exact syntax and implementation rules.

items.title: Dadrock
items.text:
Warning

dadrock is under heavy development — pre-alpha release. Expect breaking changes.

DADR is the standard: the decision record format and the project vocabulary.

dadrock is a Rust tool that implements DADR. It previews, creates, edits, and validates decision records, and it can direct local LLM agents through tasks on the decision ledger. Everything it writes is a Markdown file you could have written yourself.

dadrock init
dadrock new "Decision title"
dadrock preview
dadrock accept ID
dadrock validate

Running dadrock without a subcommand prints help. preview starts the local web server, normally at port 4004. See Install for building the binary.

items.title: Project layout
items.text:
The DADR format does not mandate a directory structure. dadrock uses this one, created by dadrock init:

dadr/
  accepted/
    01938b8e4d70-income-preprocessing.md
    01938b8f9d71-drop-missing-treatment.md
  candidates/
    01938ba1c4f3-country-exclusions.md
  rejected/
    01938b8d9c10-deprecated-cohort-filter.md
  templates/
    candidate.md                                    # optional
  tasks/
  runs/
    .gitignore
Directory Contents dadr/candidates/ Proposals awaiting review dadr/accepted/ Accepted decisions, including those later replaced dadr/rejected/ Rejected proposals dadr/templates/ Optional template overrides for new candidates dadr/tasks/ Optional project-specific agent workflows (dadr/tasks/<task-id>/task.toml plus its prompt file) dadr/runs/ Agent-run inputs, results, and logs; ignored by version control

dadrock accept changes a candidate's status to accepted and moves the file to dadr/accepted/. dadrock reject changes it to rejected and moves it to dadr/rejected/. The id never changes. dadrock supersede appends the new record's id to the old record's successors and leaves both files in dadr/accepted/.

The directory is a convenience: status in the front matter is authoritative. dadrock validate warns when a record sits in a directory that does not match its status. Use dadrock config to inspect the resolved layout. Keep the record directories in version control; run state may contain pasted context and source excerpts and is ignored by default.

items.title: First decision
items.text:
Five minutes from an empty project to one accepted decision. You do not need an agent or tags.

Change to the project where you keep your analysis, then run:

dadrock init
dadrock new "Exclude observations without treatment assignment"

init creates a dadr/ directory without overwriting existing records. new prints the location of a candidate Markdown file and generates its ID.

Start the web interface and open the local URL printed in your terminal:

dadrock preview

The candidate is waiting in the Inbox. Open it, choose Edit, and fill in its four sections (or edit the Markdown file in your usual editor):

  • Context: Some observations lack treatment assignment.
  • Decision: Exclude those observations from this analysis.
  • Alternatives: Recover assignment from the original log; explain whether this was possible.
  • Consequences: Report how many observations were removed and consider whether missingness affects interpretation.

Replace these illustrative statements with what actually happened in your project. In particular, explain why you chose this approach.

Check that the record describes your analysis accurately and that you endorse the rationale. Save your edits, then choose Accept. The record moves to dadr/accepted/, keeping its ID, and appears in the Ledger. Commit it with your analysis code. You can also accept from a terminal with dadrock accept ID, replacing ID with the candidate's ID or an unambiguous prefix.

Find it again later:

dadrock list --status accepted
dadrock validate

For a disposable example instead of your own analysis, run dadrock demo --example candidate-review /tmp/dadr-example, then dadrock preview /tmp/dadr-example. The demo requires a new or empty target directory.

items.title: Changing a decision
items.text:
When an accepted choice changes, use Supersede on the record in the web interface to prepare a replacement. The original stays as history, and accepting the replacement links the two. Dadrock records the pending replacement in an optional Markdown section:

## Replaces

[[01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333|Previous decision]]

The link uses the original record's full UUID. Keep this section if the candidate should replace that decision: it preserves the intended relationship after reloading or accepting through the CLI. On acceptance, Dadrock validates the predecessor and updates its successors together with accepting the replacement, preserving the old body. This is a Dadrock convention, not an additional required section of the DADR format.

For two records that are already accepted, dadrock supersede --from OLD --to NEW links the replacement explicitly.

items.title: Validation
items.text:
dadrock validate
dadrock validate --json

Current validation checks:

  • no date key or ISO 8601 date/time values in front matter;
  • YAML fields, UUIDv7 IDs, four sections each appearing exactly once with text, and status/location consistency;
  • duplicate full IDs and short IDs, and filename collisions;
  • missing or invalid successors and cycles in replacement relationships;
  • broken or ambiguous record wikilinks and missing local Markdown-link targets;
  • malformed tags and unreadable candidate templates.

Focused commands are dadrock validate records, dadrock validate links, and dadrock validate tags. Use labeled links such as [[01938c20a3b4|sampling rule]] to make raw Markdown easier to read.

Validation checks the records' structure and internal references. It does not compare accepted records with Git history, resolve bibliography citations, detect TBD prose, enforce plan-deviation sections, or determine whether code follows a decision. Those checks are roadmap work. Human review remains necessary.

items.title: Continuous integration
items.text: Once Dadrock is installed in your CI environment, run dadrock validate from the analysis project root. A nonzero exit status signals an error; --json provides structured diagnostics. Install from a pinned source revision for reproducibility; a CLI-only CI build can use the no-js-build feature.

items.title: Web interface
items.text:
dadrock preview
dadrock preview --port 4005 path/to/project

Open the local URL printed in the terminal. The interface has three places, side by side in the header: Inbox, Ledger, and Draft.

items.title: Inbox
items.text:
The Inbox is the home screen and the work queue. Everything that needs a human lands here, grouped by kind:

  • Candidates wait for a decision. Read the record, fix its explanation if needed, then Accept or Reject. Revise with agent sends it back to a local agent with your instructions.
  • Agent proposals are decisions a local agent drafted from your notes or your code. Save as candidate writes the file so you can review it like any other candidate; Discard drops it.
  • Proposed revisions show an agent's edit to an existing record as a diff. Apply writes it; Discard drops it.
  • Conflicts come from Check for conflicts, which asks the agent to look for overlapping or contradictory decisions. From a conflict you can Merge two candidates, Replace an accepted decision, or Dismiss the finding.
  • Issues are validation findings: structure, links, tags, and project layout. Validation runs on every load, so there is nothing to trigger. Open record jumps to the editor; Fix with agent asks for a revision; warnings and notes can be dismissed.

Review both the observed choice and its rationale. An agent-generated description of code may be accurate while the reason for that choice remains unknown. Supply the missing rationale before accepting.

An empty Inbox is the goal. The search box narrows the queue to matching titles, tags, paths, and messages. Use j and k to move through items, a and r for the primary and secondary action, e to edit, and o to open the record in the Ledger.

Record text is edited in a CodeMirror editor with Markdown and front-matter highlighting, search (Ctrl+F), and Ctrl+S to save.

items.title: Ledger
items.text: The Ledger is what has been decided. It lists accepted records, newest first, with one search box and a tag facet. Show history reveals superseded and rejected records. Each record shows its supersession chain, an inline editor, and two verbs: Supersede prepares a replacement, and Revise with agent asks a local agent to rewrite the record from your instructions. The result appears in the Inbox as a proposed revision.

items.title: Draft
items.text:
Draft is the third place: a full page reached from the header or from any record. Describe the decision in the text box, or attach files and folders to have a configured agent look for decisions in your code. Attach two candidates to merge them. Opened from a record, the same page revises or replaces that record. Results land in the Inbox as proposals.

Without an agent, Write it by hand gives you a plain form with the candidate template. Replace with existing decisions instead links an accepted record to records that already exist.

items.title: Project
items.text:
The project name in the header opens a small panel with the project root, the detected agent, and three actions: initialize a new project, run validation now, and clear the agent's run history. Local run state is stored under dadr/runs/ and ignored by default because it may contain pasted context, source excerpts, and model transcripts.

Old links still work: /records, /candidates/new, /tasks, /validation, /tags, and /settings redirect to the Inbox, the Ledger, or the Draft page.

items.title: Editor integration
items.text: The repository contains one extension implementation in editors/vscode. It provides Dadrock integration for VS Code, with a build/install target for Positron using the same extension source; see Install. This does not imply published marketplace packages or separate official extensions for Cursor, RStudio, or Neovim. You can edit DADR Markdown files in any editor and run dadrock preview alongside it.

items.title: LLM agents
items.text:
Agents are optional. Once a local agent is configured, start with a small batch of consequential choices:

dadrock task run code-to-record --path analysis/ --limit 5
dadrock task run context-to-record --context "Document why we exclude rows without treatment assignment"

Agent outputs are proposals for review. Code can show what happened without establishing why; correct unsupported claims and supply missing rationale before acceptance. The web interface offers the same drafting actions. See LLM agents for provider configuration, custom tasks, and MCP integration.

DADR decision records and web review UI.

Usage: dadrock [COMMAND]

items.title: Subcommands:
items.text:
• help — Show top-level help or detailed metadata for one command.
  • commands — List command metadata for automation and command discovery.
  • completions — Generate a shell completion script.
  • dir — Print the discovered accepted records directory.
  • config — Print the resolved project layout.
  • init — Create a Dadrock dadr/ directory.
  • demo — Seed a new project with a named DADR example.
  • new — Create a candidate decision record from the active candidate template.
  • list — List records, optionally filtered by lifecycle status, tag, or query.
  • status — Inspect one record's lifecycle status or run lifecycle transitions.
  • accept — Accept a candidate decision.
  • reject — Reject a candidate decision.
  • supersede — Link replacement decisions to the decisions they replace.
  • validate — Run project validation, or target records, links, or tags.
  • tags — Inspect DADR tag usage.
  • mcp — Serve Dadrock MCP tools over stdio.
  • agent — Call a configured local ACP agent for candidate drafting.
  • task — Discover, inspect, and run Dadrock task packages.
  • preview — Serve the local web review UI.

• --port <PORT>

Default value: 4004 * --host <HOST>

items.title: Install
items.text: Dadrock is a single binary. The web interface is embedded in it, so a complete build needs Rust and Bun; a CLI-only build needs Rust alone.

items.title: From source
items.text:
Clone the repository and build with Cargo:

git clone https://github.com/vincentarelbundock/dadr.git
cd dadr
DADROCK_REQUIRE_JS_BUILD=1 cargo install --path crates/dadrock --bin dadrock
dadrock --version

The first build downloads dependencies and may take several minutes. DADROCK_REQUIRE_JS_BUILD=1 makes the build fail rather than silently skip the web interface when Bun is missing.

items.title: Without the web interface
items.text:
For servers and continuous integration, build the command line only:

cargo install --path crates/dadrock --bin dadrock --features no-js-build

dadrock preview then shows a notice instead of the interface; every other command works. Install from a pinned revision for reproducibility.

items.title: Editor integration
items.text: The repository ships a VS Code extension under editors/vscode. From a checkout, make vscode builds the binary and the extension and installs it with the VS Code CLI; make positron targets Positron. These targets need the editor CLI, Rust, Bun, and Node. You can also edit DADR files in any editor and run dadrock preview alongside it.

items.title: Optional: a local agent
items.text: Drafting and conflict checks use a local agent speaking the Agent Client Protocol, such as claude-agent-acp. Dadrock detects one on PATH automatically; see LLM agents to configure a specific provider. Nothing else in Dadrock depends on it.

items.title: Next
items.text: Record your first decision with the software, or read what a Data Analysis Decision Record is.

items.title: LLM agents
items.text: Agent assistance is optional. The first decision needs only Dadrock. This page is for configuring an agent or integrating Dadrock into other tools.

items.title: Configure one local agent
items.text:
Dadrock connects to a locally installed agent through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). The agent may use a remote model. You need an ACP-compatible provider or bridge and its authentication. Built-in tasks include their own instructions; no separately installed skill is required. An ordinary claude or codex executable alone is not necessarily an ACP provider.

Use your provider's own installation and authentication instructions. Choose a bridge explicitly supported by your agent provider. Dadrock does not install providers or manage their credentials.

For optional guidance outside built-in tasks, copy skills/dadr/ from this checkout to your agent's supported skill directory, such as .agents/skills/dadr or ~/.codex/skills/dadr. The agent's own discovery rules determine which location works.

Check the connection:

dadrock agent check
dadrock agent skills

When more than one provider is available, choose one explicitly with --agent. Provider-specific arguments can be passed with --agent-arg. agent skills lists optional local instructions. Built-in task runs do not require a skill-loading preflight.

items.title: Draft for review
items.text:
dadrock task run code-to-record --path analysis/ --limit 5
dadrock task run context-to-record --context "Explain our choice of sample restrictions"

The limit asks the agent to prioritize a small batch, rather than treating every operation as a decision. It is a drafting request, not a hard guarantee on model output. Outputs remain proposals. Do not infer motivation from implementation alone; supply missing rationale before accepting.

Tool permission requests default to deny. When your selected workflow needs tools, explicitly choose the appropriate permission mode with --permission allow-once or --permission allow-always. This does not authorize an agent to accept decisions on your behalf.

dadrock agent draft remains available for compatibility. New workflows should use task run context-to-record.

items.title: Custom workflows and run history
items.text:
dadrock task list
dadrock task show code-to-record
dadrock task runs
dadrock task result RUN_ID

Built-in workflows include drafting, editing candidates, proposing replacements, merging drafts, finding conflicts, and synthesizing accepted decisions. Project overrides live in dadr/tasks/<task-id>/, with a task.toml manifest and a prompt file. Inspect an existing task before customizing it. Advanced and third-party inputs can use --input-json; do not combine it with friendly input flags such as --path or --context.

Runs are persisted under dadr/runs/, which is ignored by default and may contain source excerpts or model transcripts. Output kinds determine how results are rendered. Protocol and run metadata stay outside record front matter.

items.title: Integrate another agent client
items.text:
Dadrock exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server:

dadrock mcp serve
dadrock mcp serve --read-only

The normal server exposes inspection and mutation tools through the same command layer as the CLI. Use read-only mode for clients that should only inspect records. Human approval is still required for acceptance or rejection.

Dadrock attaches MCP to its agent sessions by default. --no-mcp disables that attachment for clients where it is unsuitable. These integration settings are not required to write or review records manually.

Future automated faithfulness and coverage checks are described on the roadmap.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
These are proposed directions, not currently available guarantees or delivery commitments. See Dadrock for current capabilities.

  • Change detection: inspect Git diffs and suggest consequential choices worth documenting.
  • Code-comment scanning: resolve #dadr/ annotations in analysis source files.
  • Faithfulness checks: compare accepted decisions with code, analysis plans, and manuscripts; report discrepancies for human review.
  • Reporting: draft methods sections and decision narratives with references to records.
  • Coverage and robustness: identify undocumented choices and possible sensitivity analyses.
  • Process metrics: compute review latency, coverage, and follow-through from appropriate lifecycle data.
  • Additional validation: citation resolution, plan-deviation requirements, placeholder detection, and history-based checks for substantive changes to accepted records.

Future checks should help people investigate discrepancies. A missing link does not establish that an analysis is wrong, and a clean validation report does not establish scientific correctness.

items.title: DADR specification
items.text:
For a short introduction, see Data Analysis Decision Records. Suggested tag vocabularies are documented separately.

DADR (Data-Analysis Decision Records) is a file-first format for recording consequential decisions in empirical and data-analysis projects. A DADR record is a Markdown file that captures one analytic decision: the context that motivated it, the decision that was made, the alternatives considered, and the consequences for the analysis. Records live alongside the analysis code, manuscript, data references, and project documentation.

This page is the canonical specification of the record format. Directory layouts, inference, version-control hooks, previews, and agent workflows are tooling concerns; the reference implementation documents its own choices in the dadrock section.

items.title: Version
items.text:
This document defines DADR specification version 0.1.0-alpha.2.

DADR uses Semantic Versioning. Versions below 1.0.0 are alpha-stage specifications: breaking changes MAY appear in minor or patch releases while the model is still being validated. Starting with 1.0.0, breaking changes MUST increment the major version.

items.title: 1. Conventions
items.text:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, and MAY are normative when written in uppercase. Examples are non-normative.

Record — one Markdown file with DADR front matter and a body.

Record set — the records a tool is pointed at, such as all records in a project. Every rule that relates records to one another (unique identifiers, resolving links, supersession) is evaluated over the record set. This specification does not mandate where record files live.

items.title: 2. Records
items.text:
A record MUST describe exactly one decision or one proposed decision. Closely related choices SHOULD be split into separate records when they could be accepted, rejected, or superseded independently.

A record MUST be a single UTF-8 Markdown file without a byte-order mark. It consists of YAML front matter followed by a Markdown body.

The Markdown file is the source of truth. Indexes, databases, graphs, reports, and static sites built from records are derived and not canonical. Records MUST remain readable and editable with an ordinary text editor; tools are a convenience, not a requirement.

items.title: 3. Front matter
items.text:
A record MUST begin with YAML front matter delimited by --- lines. The front matter MUST be a YAML mapping with these keys:

Key Required Value title yes A non-empty, single-line string: a short noun phrase. 120 characters or fewer is recommended. status yes candidate, accepted, or rejected. See Lifecycle. id yes A UUIDv7 in lowercase hyphenated form. See Identifiers. successors no An array of ids of the accepted records that supersede this one. See Supersession. tags no An array of tags, written without the leading #. See Tags.

An omitted array and an empty array ([]) are equivalent.

Front matter MUST NOT record dates or times. A record's time is always derived from its id (Identifiers). In particular, front matter MUST NOT contain a date key, nor, under any key, a value written as an ISO 8601 date or date-time, such as 2026-05-07 or 2026-05-07T14:30:00Z.

Other keys MAY appear, for example author, aliases, or Pandoc's bibliography. They carry no DADR meaning. Tools MUST NOT reject a record because of them unless they break the date rule above, and tools that rewrite front matter MUST preserve them.

DADR expresses classifications such as kind, confidence, provenance, topic, or the people involved as tags rather than as dedicated keys. The Tags page suggests a vocabulary.

---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: candidate
id: 01938b8f-9d71-7456-8000-fedcba987654
tags:
  - kind/sample
  - writer/agent
---

items.title: 4. Body
items.text:
An accepted record MUST contain exactly one ## heading for each of the four standard sections. Headings match case-insensitively. A section's content runs from its heading to the next # or ## heading.

## Context

What problem, dataset, or constraint motivated this decision?

## Decision

What was decided? State the choice in one or two sentences, in the active voice.

## Alternatives

What other options were considered, and why were they set aside?

## Consequences

What follows for results, downstream analyses, robustness checks, or future work?

In an accepted record, each standard section MUST contain text other than whitespace and HTML comments. When nothing applies, say so in words; for example, "No alternatives were considered."

The sections MAY appear in any order. Records MAY add other sections, such as ## Robustness, ## Plan deviation, or ## Open questions. A candidate MAY omit or leave empty any section; the requirements above apply once it is accepted.

The four sections follow Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), a common software-engineering practice for capturing the context, choice, and consequences of a design decision in a short Markdown file. DADR applies the same structure to data analysis.

items.title: 5. Identifiers and filenames
items.text:
A record's id is a UUIDv7 (RFC 9562) written in lowercase canonical form (8-4-4-4-12, 36 characters). It is assigned when the record is created and never changes, including when the record is accepted or rejected. The id is the record's only stable key: titles, filenames, and locations may change.

UUIDv7 needs no shared counter, so concurrent branches and agents can create records safely. Its first 48 bits are a Unix-millisecond timestamp, so identifiers sort by creation time. That timestamp is the record's only date: records never store another one (§3). When a record was accepted, rejected, or superseded, and by whom, belongs to version control or tool logs, not to the record.

The short id is the first 12 hexadecimal digits of the id, with no hyphen:

id:        01938b8e-4d70-7abc-8def-0123456789ab
short id:  01938b8e4d70

Short ids MUST be unique within a record set. Tools that create records MUST ensure this, for example by generating a fresh id when the short id is already taken.

A record's filename SHOULD be its short id, a hyphen, a short kebab-case slug of its title, and .md:

01938b8e4d70-income-preprocessing.md

Authors drafting by hand can take an id from the UUID v7 generator. A file without an id is not a valid record; tools MAY repair it by assigning a fresh id.

items.title: 6.1 Status
items.text:
Status Meaning candidate A proposed decision under review. accepted A human-approved decision, whether or not it has since been superseded. rejected A candidate closed without approval: rejected, withdrawn, duplicated, merged into another record, or no longer relevant.

The only transitions are candidate → accepted and candidate → rejected. Each changes the status of the same record and keeps its id. accepted and rejected are final. To revisit a rejected or superseded decision, create a new candidate.

A record's lifecycle stage is given by its status alone. Tools MUST NOT infer it from the file's name or location.

Acceptance is a human decision. Tools and agents MUST NOT accept a candidate without human approval, and a candidate MUST meet the body requirements to be accepted.

items.title: 6.2 Supersession
items.text:
To replace an accepted decision, accept a new record and add its id to the old record's successors. An accepted record with a non-empty successors array is superseded. This is derived from the record set; it is not a status, and the old record's status stays accepted.

successors:
  - 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333

Within a record set:

  • only accepted records MAY have a non-empty successors array;
  • each entry MUST be the id of an accepted record other than the record itself;
  • the graph formed by successors MUST be acyclic.

successors is an array, so one decision can be split into several successors, and several decisions can share one successor. Only the forward edge is stored; tools derive predecessors by scanning the record set. Supersession exists only in successors: a mention in prose or a wikilink does not supersede a record.

items.title: 6.3 Immutability
items.text:
Candidates MAY be edited freely. Once a record is accepted:

  • its id and status MUST NOT change, and entries MUST NOT be removed from successors;
  • the meaning of its title and body MUST NOT change. Corrections that leave the meaning intact, such as fixing spelling, formatting, links, or citations, are allowed.

tags and keys outside DADR MAY change. To change an accepted decision, create a new candidate, accept it, and supersede the old record.

The first rule can be checked mechanically, for example against version-control history. The second requires a reviewer's judgment.

items.title: 7. Tags
items.text:
DADR uses the Obsidian tag syntax:

  • in body text, a tag begins with #; in the front-matter tags array, it is written without #;
  • a tag consists of Unicode letters, numbers, emoji, _, -, and /, and contains no whitespace;
  • / separates levels of a hierarchy, so kind/sample is a child of kind; empty levels (a//b, a/, /a) are invalid;
  • a tag MUST contain at least one character other than a digit, _, -, or /, so #1984 is invalid and #y1984 is valid;
  • tags are case-insensitive: #Kind and #kind are the same tag.

DADR defines no required tag vocabulary. Projects choose their own; the Tags page suggests one.

Front-matter tags classify the whole record. Inline tags in the body attach to the passage they appear in; a common pattern is the first line of a blockquote. Tools SHOULD treat both as one tag set when indexing or reporting.

> #confidence/low
> The pre-analysis plan called for a complete-case rule. We now prefer multiple
> imputation, pending a check of missingness by site.

items.title: 7.1 Code tags
items.text:
In source-code comments, DADR tags carry a #dadr/ prefix that separates them from other comment text and other tag systems:

# #dadr/01938b8e4d70
df <- df[!is.na(df$treatment), ]

# #dadr/kind/measurement #dadr/topic/student-survey
survey["anx_mean"] = survey[["anx1", "anx2", "anx3"]].mean(axis=1)
  • #dadr/ followed by a short id or full id links the nearby code to that record. A link that does not resolve to a record in the record set is broken, and tools that check code tags SHOULD report it.
  • #dadr/ followed by any other tag annotates the nearby code with that tag; for example, #dadr/kind/measurement carries the tag kind/measurement.

Which lines of code a tag covers is defined by the tools that read it. Tags inside record files do not use the #dadr/ prefix.

items.title: 8.1 Links between records
items.text:
A wikilink whose target is a short id or a full id is a record link:

See [[01938c20a3b4]] for the sampling rule.
Compare with [[01938b8e4d70|the original preprocessing decision]].

The short id form is recommended. Hexadecimal digits match case-insensitively. A record link MUST resolve to a record in the record set, and tools MUST report links that do not resolve rather than guess a target. The form [[target|display text]] sets the displayed text.

Wikilinks with any other target are not DADR links, and tools MUST leave them unchanged. Tools MAY convert record links to ordinary Markdown links when rendering, for renderers that do not support wikilinks.

items.title: 8.2 Other links
items.text:
References to code, data, notebooks, manuscripts, plans, outputs, registries, and web pages SHOULD be standard Markdown links or autolinks, which every renderer supports. Relative paths resolve from the directory that contains the record, as in any Markdown renderer.

The exclusion is enforced in
[`analysis/build_sample.py` lines 42–58](../../analysis/build_sample.py#L42-L58),
following the pre-registration at <https://osf.io/abcde>.

items.title: 8.3 Citations
items.text: Records MAY cite sources with Pandoc citation syntax, such as [@rubin1976]. Resolving citation keys is up to the renderer. A Pandoc bibliography key in front matter is treated like any other key outside DADR.

items.title: 9. Conformance
items.text:
A record conforms if:

  1. it is a UTF-8 Markdown file without a byte-order mark, beginning with YAML front matter that is a mapping;
  2. title, status, and id are present and valid (§3, §5);
  3. the front matter contains no date key and no ISO 8601 date or date-time value (§3);
  4. successors, if present, is an array of UUIDv7 ids, and is empty unless status is accepted;
  5. tags, if present, is an array of valid tags (§7);
  6. if status is accepted, the body meets §4.

A record set conforms if every record in it conforms and:

  1. no two records share an id or a short id;
  2. every successors entry names another accepted record, and the successors graph is acyclic (§6.2);
  3. every record link resolves (§8.1).

A tool conforms if it:

  1. identifies records by id and lifecycle stage by status, never by filename or location;
  2. reports violations of these rules instead of silently guessing or repairing them;
  3. preserves front-matter keys it does not use when it rewrites a record;
  4. creates records with unique short ids;
  5. never accepts a candidate without human approval, and changes accepted records only as §6.3 allows.

A filename that does not follow §5 does not make a record non-conforming.

items.title: 10. Example record
items.text:
This example is non-normative.

---
title: Drop observations with missing treatment assignment
status: accepted
id: 01938c20-a3b4-7000-8000-111122223333
tags:
  - kind/sample
---

# Drop observations with missing treatment assignment

## Context

The treatment variable is required for the primary estimand. Observations with
missing treatment assignment cannot contribute to the main comparison without
introducing an additional imputation model. See [[01938b8e4d70]] for how the
analysis sample was first defined.

## Decision

Drop observations with missing treatment assignment from the main analysis
sample.

## Alternatives

One alternative was to impute treatment assignment. This was not chosen because
the assignment mechanism is part of the study design rather than a downstream
measurement, and imputing it would make the estimand harder to interpret.

Another alternative was to keep the observations for descriptive tables only.
This can still be done in a supplemental descriptive analysis, but those rows
are excluded from the primary model.

## Consequences

The main sample size decreases. The manuscript should report the number of
excluded observations, and robustness checks should verify that treatment
missingness is not concentrated in one site.

items.title: Reference implementation
items.text: The reference implementation is dadrock, a Rust tool with a CLI, a web UI, and IDE integrations. See the dadrock section for its project layout, commands, and validation, and the Tags page for the recommended tag vocabulary.

items.title: Tags
items.text: You can use DADR without tags. Add them when they help your team find related decisions; there is no mandatory vocabulary.

items.title: Start small
items.text:
These are suggested conventions, not reserved fields or required categories:

Tag Meaning kind/sample Sample definition or inclusion rules kind/modeling Model choices kind/inference Uncertainty and tests writer/agent An agent helped draft the record people/decider/alice Person responsible for the choice people/approver/bob Person who reviewed and approved it people/reviewer/bob Optional project convention for a reviewer axis/sample/complete-case A choice along a robustness or specification axis multiverse/model/ols Another project convention for an alternative specification rejected/duplicate Why a candidate was closed

Use project-specific tags when they are useful. Existing vocabularies remain valid; there is no need to migrate records just to follow these examples.

items.title: Where to put them
items.text:
In YAML front matter, omit the leading #:

tags:
  - kind/sample
  - people/decider/alice

In prose, include it:

The exclusion rule is one sensitivity-analysis option. #axis/sample/complete-case

Use one spelling per concept and avoid near-duplicates. See the specification for exact syntax and normalization rules.

items.title: Inspect and validate
items.text:
dadrock tags list
dadrock validate tags

The specification also describes #dadr/ annotations in code comments. Dadrock does not currently scan or validate those source annotations; that is roadmap work.

items.title: Optional code annotations
items.text:
These conventions describe future tooling; Dadrock does not yet scan source comments.

In source-code comments, prefix tags with #dadr/. The same namespaces apply:

Pattern Meaning #dadr/<short-id> Link the surrounding code to a record, e.g. #dadr/01938c20a3b4. A full UUID also works. #dadr/kind/<value> The kind of decision the code implements. #dadr/topic/<value> Free-form topic. #dadr/plan/<id> The plan item the code implements. #dadr/multiverse/<axis>/<value> The value of a robustness or specification axis implemented here. #dadr/confidence/<low\|medium\|high> Author confidence in the annotation.

Several tags can share one comment:

-- #dadr/kind/sample #dadr/topic/missingness
where treatment is not null

items.title: UUID v7 generator
items.text:
Every DADR record should have a UUID v7 in its front-matter id field. The record filename should normally begin with the first 12 hex characters of that identifier, followed by a short kebab-case title.

You may use this page when you are drafting DADR records by hand and need a fresh identifier.

Generate UUID v7

Full UUIDv7 Copy UUID DADR filename prefix Copy prefix

This generator runs entirely in your browser. It writes the current Unix millisecond timestamp into the UUIDv7 timestamp field and fills the remaining random bits with crypto.getRandomValues().
